title: Research Review: AI+Human Tutors Match Quality of Human-Only Tutors?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer reviews a high-profile UK exploratory RCT -- Eedi and Google DeepMind's study embedding three kinds of tutoring support (static pre-written hints, human chat support, and AI-drafted chat support supervised by a human tutor) inside the Eedi math platform -- and works through what the results do and don't actually show. Both dynamic support conditions beat static hints, as expected, but the more interesting finding is that human-only and human+AI support performed similarly on immediate measures (mistake remediation, misconception resolution), while human+AI showed a 5.5% edge specifically on 'knowledge transfer,' a result Meyer finds genuinely surprising and flags as a possible case of researchers hunting for significance across multiple outcome measures. Meyer is careful to separate what's reassuring here (human supervision of AI messages, 76% accepted without significant edits, no degradation in learning even where there's no improvement) from what's not: this was a small, short intervention (seven hours over seven weeks) on proprietary measures, and the entire model of 'tutoring via text chat' already discards much of what makes human tutoring effective in the first place -- in-person, relationship-based, curriculum-aligned support. He closes by linking the study to two other current AI-in-education data points -- a University of Washington student's op-ed on near-universal AI use on campus, and Austin ISD's use of AI for master scheduling -- to argue AI's more defensible near-term role is operational support rather than in-classroom relational teaching.
points: Meyer's sharpest analytical move is distinguishing what was actually measured from what sounds like it was measured: the human+AI advantage showed up specifically on 'knowledge transfer' rather than the more intuitive immediate measures, which he finds surprising enough to flag as possible p-hacking risk.

He offers a memorable analogy for why text-chat tutoring undersells human tutoring's real strengths: 'It's as if we asked Michael Bublé to play the kazoo and then supervise a robot purpose-built to play a kazoo' -- the comparison discards what makes in-person human tutoring valuable in the first place.

Meyer flags the practical scale of the intervention as a limiting factor often lost in headline framing: seven hours total, one hour per week over seven weeks, is enough to shift 'proprietary measures' but not to sustain claims about a broader school-improvement strategy.

He treats the human-supervision structure (tutors approving, editing, or rewriting 76% of AI-drafted messages without significant changes) as a genuinely reassuring safety detail, distinguishing this study's design from riskier 'AI directly to kids' models.

His closing frame -- pairing this tutoring study with Austin ISD's use of AI for master scheduling -- makes an explicit argument that AI's more defensible current role is 'back-office operational tasks' rather than 'the in-classroom relational work of teaching.'
quotes: The researchers embedded three kinds of support inside Eedi, a math software platform. Support #1: Static pre-written hints. Support #2: A chat interface for accessing support from a human. Support #3: A chat interface for accessing support from an LLM, with a human approving the messages.
The study stored the original AI responses and the edits from human tutors (a fun source of data) which led to the finding that 76% of the LLM responses were accepted in full by the human tutor.
It's a small practical effect in a short intervention. The total time here was seven hours -- one hour per week over seven weeks -- for an increase of 5.5% on some proprietary measures.

It’s as if we asked Michael Bublé to play the kazoo and then supervise a robot purpose-built to play a kazoo. I’m not sure we’d be surprised by the results. I’m also not sure we’d feel good about saying “AI+Michael Bublé Match Quality Of Michael Bublé Alone.

It’s honestly quite strange to me that the Human + LLM showed its strengths with “Knowledge Transfer.” I would have expected to see the greatest difference on follow-up tasks that were closer to the tutoring moment.

I don’t hold up “time savings” as a first-order goal for teachers, administrators, or schools. There are plenty of ways to save time that result in a worse education for kids. But I am much more optimistic that AI can support back-office operational tasks like this rather than the in-classroom relational work of teaching.
